title: spec.jobTemplate.spec.podFailurePolicy.rules[0].onPodConditions[0].status: Required value: valid values: ["False" "True" "Unknown"]
body:
### What happened?

When I try to apply (patching) an existing `CronJob` with the following `podFailurePolicy`:
```
      podFailurePolicy:
        rules:
        - action: Ignore
          onPodConditions:
          - type: DisruptionTarget
```

I'm getting the following Error:
```
error when patching "/dev/shm/2794561279": CronJob.batch "mycronjob" is invalid: spec.jobTemplate.spec.podFailurePolicy.rules[0].onPodConditions[0].status: Required value: valid values: ["False" "True" "Unknown"]
```


Following the docs ([link1](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2024/08/19/kubernetes-1-31-pod-failure-policy-for-jobs-goes-ga/), [link2](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2024/08/19/kubernetes-1-31-pod-failure-policy-for-jobs-goes-ga/)), it seems to be optional.

same in code(?)

https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/c5439348b1cf0e96c7446a1bef9475553530f12f/batch/v1/types.go#L214


### What did you expect to happen?

should be applied without any errors

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

create a sample cronjob with these configurations: 

```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: mycronjob
  labels:
    app: release-name
    app.kubernetes.io/name: "release-name"
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: "release-name"
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: mycronjob
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  suspend: false
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 100
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 2
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 172800 
      backoffLimit: 2
      parallelism: 1
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 1800
      podFailurePolicy:
        rules:
        - action: Ignore
          onPodConditions:
          - type: DisruptionTarget
...
```

### Anything else we need to know?

workaround: adding the field `status: 'True'` fix it

```
    podFailurePolicy:
      rules:
      - action: Ignore
        onPodConditions:
        - type: DisruptionTarget
          status: 'True'
```

```console
v1.31.7-eks-bcf3d70
```

title: [WINDOWS] [KUBEPROXY] HNS LoadBalancer Fails to Update Endpoints After ModifyLoadBalancerAPI Invocation by Windows KubeProxy
body:
### What happened?

I'm using HNS version 15.4, where the ModifyLoadBalancer policy appears to be supported according to hnslib. KubeProxy is invoking the ModifyLoadBalancer API, but the endpoints it attempts to update do not match those reflected in HNS.

### What did you expect to happen?

Following the ModifyLoadBalancer API call, all the requested endpoints should be successfully updated in HNS.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create an AKS cluster with 1.31+ version of K8S and Windows OS version 2025
- Create a deployment and a loadbalancer service for the deployment.
- Check the endpoint list count in the newly create hns loadbalancer policy.
- Scale up the pods for the deployment and check the endpoint list count for the same hns lob policy. It will still show the old endpoint list.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: HPA watch pod metrics calls fail with 422 error code
body:
### What happened? HorizontalPodAutoscaler is making failed `watch` requests for pod metrics, then falling back to `list` calls which are successful. This doesn't immediately impact functionality but the extra failed requests can cause unnecessary load and skew metrics. __Request Details__ key | value -- | -- verb | watch requestURI | /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/default/pods?allowWatchBookmarks=true&labelSelector=run%3Dphp-apache&resourceVersionMatch=NotOlderThan&sendInitialEvents=true&watch=true responseStatus.code | 422 user.username | system:serviceaccount:kube-system:horizontal-pod-autoscaler userAgent | kube-controller-manager/v1.32.3 (linux/amd64) kubernetes/470a1dd/system:serviceaccount:kube-system:horizontal-pod-autoscaler `kube-controller-manager` logs have the following error: ``` 13 type.go:183] The watchlist request for pods ended with an error, falling back to the standard LIST semantics, err = ListOptions.meta.k8s.io "" is invalid: [resourceVersionMatch: Forbidden: resourceVersionMatch is forbidden for watch, resourceVersionMatch: Forbidden: resourceVersionMatch is forbidden unless resourceVersion is provided] ``` It appears that the watch request is missing a required `resourceVersion` parameter. ### What did you expect to happen? The watch pod metrics calls to succeed. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Create an HPA in a 1.32 cluster via https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale-walkthrough/ * start metrics server * `kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/application/php-apache.yaml ` * `kubectl autoscale deployment php-apache --cpu-percent=50 --min=1 --max=10` Observe audit logs for 422 errors. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
kube-controller-manager/v1.32.3

title: NodeResizePending status not removed after successful NodeExpandVolume
body:
### What happened?

When resizing a Persistent Disk CSI driver-backed volume, although the node expansion succeeds and the CSI driver completes NodeExpandVolume, the PVC's AllocatedResourceStatus NodeResizePending condition persists.

```
 spec:
    accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 15Gi
    storageClassName: standard-rwo
    volumeMode: Filesystem
    volumeName: pvc-22d448b9-d98a-46d5-9910-fd2cb0029a7d
  status:
    accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    allocatedResourceStatuses:
      storage: NodeResizePending
    allocatedResources:
      storage: 15Gi
    capacity:
      storage: 15Gi
    phase: Bound
```

Upon pod restart, the NodeExpandVolume operation successfully resizes the file system.
```
/csi.v1.Node/NodeExpandVolume returned with response: capacity_bytes:16106127360
"NodeExpandVolume succeeded on volume Key{"pvc-8fb88ce1-0feb-47c7-9993-e6bf9d0d64e7", zone: "x"} to size 16106127360"
```
Despite this, node logs show that NodeExpandVolume is failing due to an unidentified error.
```
nestedpendingoperations.go:348] Operation for "{volumeName:kubernetes.io/csi/pd.csi.storage.gke.io^projects/x/zones/x/disks/pvc-8fb88ce1-0feb-47c7-9993-e6bf9d0d64e7 podName: nodeName:}" failed. No retries permitted until 2025-04-18 20:17:09.901667408 +0000 UTC m=+10542.012736234 (durationBeforeRetry 16s). Error: NodeExpandVolume.NodeExpandVolume failed to resize volume for volume "pvc-8fb88ce1-0feb-47c7-9993-e6bf9d0d64e7" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/csi/pd.csi.storage.gke.io^projects/x/zones/x/disks/pvc-8fb88ce1-0feb-47c7-9993-e6bf9d0d64e7") pod "pod" (UID: "18e508ae-a670-4486-b993-e6355d0abcff") : volume resizing failed for unknown reason
```
The Kubelet appears to unexpectedly enter a placeholder code path. This issue can be traced to the following lines in the Kubernetes source code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/680ea07dbb2c6050d13b93660fa4d27d2d28d6eb/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L1921-L1924. 

### What did you expect to happen?

After completion of NodeExpandVolume, we expect that NodeResizePending status is removed.
```
  spec:
    accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 15Gi
    storageClassName: standard-rwo
    volumeMode: Filesystem
    volumeName: pvc-8fb88ce1-0feb-47c7-9993-e6bf9d0d64e7
  status:
    accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    allocatedResources:
      storage: 15Gi
    capacity:
      storage: 15Gi
    phase: Bound
```


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy a GKE cluster with master version `1.32.2-gke.1182003` and one node running version `1.31.6-gke.1020000`.
2. Create a pod that utilizes a `standard-rwo` PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) with an initial size of 5Gi.
3. After the pod is operational, expand the PVC's storage capacity to 15Gi.
4. Restart the pod.
5. Examine the status of the PVC.

### Anything else we need to know?

The "NodeResizePending" status resolves successfully when the node and cluster versions match at v1.31.6-gke.1020000. This issue seems to arise only when the cluster and node versions are different.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.32.2
Kustomize Version: v5.5.0
Server Version: v1.32.2-gke.1182003
```
Node version: v1.31.6-gke.1020000
Resizer version: v1.13.1-gke.0
</details>

The `failed for unknown reasons` is bit of a red herring and is similar to bug - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/131397#issuecomment-2817971686 .

This happens because PV capacity is updated by the external-resizer, but `pvc.Status.AllocatedResourceStatus` hasn't been updated to `NodeResizePending` so as kubelet can perform volume expansion. So although - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L1922 looks like an error, it is basically benign error and should clear away once volume is expanded on the kubelet.

If `allocatedResourceStatus` is stuck on `NodeResizePending`, it can't be because of aforementioned "failed for unknown reasons", error. 

To debug this further we will need more logs from kubelet and resizer. Also, can you post exact version of resizer when this happened?

>Deploy a GKE cluster with master version 1.32.2-gke.1182003 and one node running version 1.31.6-gke.1020000.

So basically kube-control-plane is on v1.32.2 but one of the nodes is still on v1.31.6.

> The resizer version was v1.13.1-gke.0, I will work on getting more logs posted here.

So, in this case problem is - external-resizer is newer and has recovery feature enabled, but one of the nodes is older and doesn't have recovery feature enabled. In which case, it doesn't know how to *remove* the `allocatedResourceStatuses` statuses, because this is only enabled in v1.32.x k8s version.

So, I strongly suspect that is why, this status is not being removed after successful completion of resizing on older node.
I think we need to have kubelet gated by field presence rather than feature gate enablement.

As a short term mitigation for clusters in this state before we have a fix, I think the steps should be:

1) Disable recovery feature in resizer
2) Manually clear the status.allocatedResourceStatuses from PVC objects

> As a short term mitigation for clusters in this state before we have a fix, I think the steps should be:

> Disable recovery feature in resizer
> Manually clear the status.allocatedResourceStatuses from PVC objects

Yes, as long as one or more nodes are still on v1.31 and cluster needs to stay that way. 

> I think we need to have kubelet gated by field presence rather than feature gate enablement.

We did this for the case where kubelet is newer but resizer is older. We need to this the other way too - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L2085

title: NodeResizeError persists after successful PVC resize with CSI drivers lacking NodeExpandVolume support
body:
### What happened?

After resizing a PVC backed by the CephFS CSI driver (which does not implement NodeExpandVolume), Kubernetes successfully performs the controller-side resize. The PVC's capacity and allocatedResources fields are updated to the correct value, and the volume is usable in the pod.

However, the PVC status remains in a NodeResizeError condition indefinitely, with a message like:

```
conditions:
- type: NodeResizeError
  status: "True"
  message: failed to expand pvc with NodeExpand is not supported by the CSI driver rook-ceph.cephfs.csi.ceph.com

```
This happens even after pod restarts and with RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure=true enabled. The error condition is cosmetic — the filesystem is resized correctly — but it is never cleared, causing persistent alerts and misleading status.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes (or the external resizer) should detect that:

*    The CSI driver does not support NodeExpandVolume

*    The resize succeeded on the controller side

*    The PVC is healthy and matches the requested size

It should then automatically clear the NodeResizeError condition.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.    Use the Rook CephFS CSI driver with a StorageClass that allows volume expansion.

2.    Ensure the CSI driver supports ControllerExpandVolume but not NodeExpandVolume.

3.    Enable RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure=true on the kube-controller-manager.

4.    Create and bind a PVC.

5.    Resize the PVC by increasing its spec.resources.requests.storage.

 6.   Wait for pod to restart or manually restart the pod.

7.    Observe that the PVC is resized (capacity and allocatedResources match), but NodeResizeError condition is never cleared.


### Anything else we need to know?

This is not a functional error — the PVC works as intended. However, the error condition misleads monitoring tools and operators. It appears that Kubernetes never recovers from a permanent NodeExpandVolume failure, even when the resize is complete and usable.

Possibly related but distinct from earlier resize error tracking issues. As of Kubernetes 1.29+, this behavior uses new condition types like NodeResizeError and NodeResizeInfeasible, but the PVC controller does not reconcile them correctly.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.32.3
Server Version: v1.32.3
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
Bare Metal / Talos Linux
</details>


### OS version

<details>

```console
Talos Linux 1.9
```

</details>


### Install tools

<details>
Talos + Flux + Helm
</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>
containerd 1.7.x (via Talos)
</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>

    CSI Driver: quay.io/cephcsi/cephcsi:v3.13.0

    External Resizer: registry.k8s.io/sig-storage/csi-resizer:v1.13.1

    Provisioner: csi-provisioner:v5.1.0

    Feature Gate: RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure=true

body:

title: Kubelet ReadOnlyPort cannot be set to 0 via golang KubeletConfiguration
body:
### What happened?

The kubelet ReadOnlyPort cannot be set to 0 via KubeletConfiguration struct.

As per the docs:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/
> **--read-only-port** int32     Default: 10255
> The read-only port for the kubelet to serve on with no authentication/authorization (set to 0 to disable).
> (DEPRECATED: This parameter should be set via the config file specified by the kubelet's --config flag. See kubelet-config-file for more information.)


https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/kubelet-config.v1beta1/#kubelet-config-k8s-io-v1beta1-KubeletConfiguration
> **readOnlyPort** int32     Default: 0 (disabled)
> readOnlyPort is the read-only port for the Kubelet to serve on with no authentication/authorization. The port number must be between 1 and 65535, inclusive. Setting this field to 0 disables the read-only service.

If you attempt to set this to 0 this using the golang struct, the field will be omitted when marshaled to YAML or JSON as the json field tag has `omitempty` and 0 is the empty value for an int32:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/35716897a3d8cd2944aa172006c5b7604a64c22e/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/config/v1beta1/types.go#L145

### What did you expect to happen?

Field is not dropped from YAML

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```golang
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	kubeletconfig "k8s.io/kubelet/config/v1beta1"
	"sigs.k8s.io/yaml"
)

func main() {
	config := &kubeletconfig.KubeletConfiguration{
		TypeMeta: metav1.TypeMeta{
			APIVersion: "kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1",
			Kind:       "KubeletConfiguration",
		},
		ReadOnlyPort: 0,
	}
	b, _ := yaml.Marshal(config)
	fmt.Printf("%s", b)
}
```
```console
brandond@dev01:~$ go run main.go
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
authentication:
  anonymous: {}
  webhook:
    cacheTTL: 0s
  x509: {}
authorization:
  webhook:
    cacheAuthorizedTTL: 0s
    cacheUnauthorizedTTL: 0s
containerRuntimeEndpoint: ""
cpuManagerReconcilePeriod: 0s
evictionPressureTransitionPeriod: 0s
fileCheckFrequency: 0s
httpCheckFrequency: 0s
imageMaximumGCAge: 0s
imageMinimumGCAge: 0s
kind: KubeletConfiguration
logging:
  flushFrequency: 0
  options:
    json:
      infoBufferSize: "0"
    text:
      infoBufferSize: "0"
  verbosity: 0
memorySwap: {}
nodeStatusReportFrequency: 0s
nodeStatusUpdateFrequency: 0s
runtimeRequestTimeout: 0s
shutdownGracePeriod: 0s
shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods: 0s
streamingConnectionIdleTimeout: 0s
syncFrequency: 0s
volumeStatsAggPeriod: 0s
```

Since the deprecated CLI flag defaults to 10255, and the field is not rendered into the configuration YAML that is passed to the kubelet, the port remains set to 10255.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is probably another case of a field that should have been *int32 instead of int32.

```console
Kustomize Version: v5.5.0

```

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/79421
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127421

cc @liggitt

> Since the deprecated CLI flag defaults to 10255, and the field is not rendered into the configuration YAML that is passed to the kubelet, the port remains set to 10255.

When reading from a config file, the field defaults to 0 as an improved security measure.

When not reading from a config file, the command-line flag defaults to 10255 for backwards compatibility with pre-config-file behavior.

@liggitt
> When reading from a config file, the field defaults to 0 as an improved security measure.

I don't believe this is accurate. If the intent was to use default to 0 whenever a config file is used (even if the config file doesn't specify a value), that is not occurring.

When the Kubelet is configured via a config file, and neither CLI flags nor config file specify the ReadOnlyPort, the effective value at runtime still defaults to 10255.

I'm trying to generate the config file using the golang struct, and I cannot do that because this field is dropped if 0 when marshaling, which results in the kubelet still operating with the port set to 10255.

> When the Kubelet is configured via a config file, and the config file does not contain the `readOnlyPort` field, the effective value at runtime still defaults to 10255 - even if the CLI flag is not present.

Starting a Kubelet with `--config=...` discards the CLI flag defaults, makes the readonly port default to 0 and be disabled by default. You can verify this by bumping log-verbosity to 5 and seeing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b53b9fb5573323484af9a19cf3f5bfe80760abba/cmd/kubelet/app/server.go#L288-L289

edit local-up-cluster.sh to omit readOnlyPort from the kubelet config it starts with:
```diff
diff --git a/hack/local-up-cluster.sh b/hack/local-up-cluster.sh
index 2bcc6f1e76e0..0e429c302418 100755
--- a/hack/local-up-cluster.sh
+++ b/hack/local-up-cluster.sh
@@ -874,7 +874,6 @@ localStorageCapacityIsolation: ${LOCAL_STORAGE_CAPACITY_ISOLATION}
 evictionPressureTransitionPeriod: "${EVICTION_PRESSURE_TRANSITION_PERIOD}"
 failSwapOn: ${FAIL_SWAP_ON}
 port: ${KUBELET_PORT}
-readOnlyPort: ${KUBELET_READ_ONLY_PORT}
 rotateCertificates: true
 runtimeRequestTimeout: "${RUNTIME_REQUEST_TIMEOUT}"
 staticPodPath: "${POD_MANIFEST_PATH}"
```

start the kubelet and view the log:
```
LOG_LEVEL=5 START_MODE=kubeletonly hack/local-up-cluster.sh 
...
more /tmp/kubelet.log
...
I0417 18:15:07.260992 2736679 server.go:285] "KubeletConfiguration" configuration=<
	{
	  "EnableServer": true,
	  "StaticPodPath": "/var/run/kubernetes/static-pods",
	  "PodLogsDir": "/var/log/pods",
	  "SyncFrequency": "1m0s",
	  "FileCheckFrequency": "20s",
	  "HTTPCheckFrequency": "20s",
	  "StaticPodURL": "",
	  "StaticPodURLHeader": null,
	  "Address": "127.0.0.1",
	  "Port": 10250,
	  "ReadOnlyPort": 0,
...
```

> Starting a Kubelet with --config=... discards the CLI flag defaults,

Ah but we're not using `--config`. We're only using `--config-dir`, which does NOT discard the CLI flag defaults. So I guess that bit is working as documented, although the nuance is easy to miss.

How should I go about generating config drop-in YAML from golang if fields are dropped during marshaling? Any possible workaround here (creating our own struct with the correct handling for this field, building yaml from strings, etc) feels like a hack.

> Ah but we're not using --config. We're only using --config-dir, which apparently does NOT discard the CLI flag defaults?

Correct. `--config-dir` merges the explicitly serialized fields read from individual drop-in files onto the base in-memory kubelet config, which either came from flags (with legacy flag defaulting readOnlyPort to 10255) or from `--config` (with improved defaulting readOnlyPort to 0).

If you want one of the overlay files in `--config-dir` to force a primitive field back to a zero-value (`""`, or `false`, or `0`) you'll need to serialize that explicitly yourself, likely not using the go type ... pretty much all the primitive fields in the KubeletConfiguration specify `omitempty`.

The alternative (explicitly serializing all the zero-value fields from the go type) would be worse... it would mean every drop in file would reset almost all fields to empty, making the merge unusable.
I'd recommend you move your base config from using CLI flags to using a `--config` file.

> you'll need to serialize that explicitly yourself, likely not using the go type

That's what I was afraid of, and trying to avoid.

> The alternative (explicitly serializing all the zero-value fields from the go type) would be worse... it would mean every drop in file would reset almost all fields to empty, making the merge unusable.

Yeah, I guess there's not a good way to handle that short of making all fields that hold primitive types pointers which would be ugly in a different way. Not the first place where it has been difficult to tell the difference between default and unset.

> I'd recommend you move your base config from using CLI flags to using a --config file.

We've already switched from CLI flags to config files, but we were aiming for maximal flexibility by only using config drop-ins. We generate a drop-in config file that sorts early, but users can decide if they want theirs to come before or after ours by naming it appropriately.
Thanks for the assist @liggitt!

Sure!

These are the other legacy defaults where CLI defaults differ from `--config` defaults, which you'll want to make sure are working as you expect:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b53b9fb5573323484af9a19cf3f5bfe80760abba/cmd/kubelet/app/options/options.go#L215-L227

Looks like the other three fields either don't need to be set to a zero-value:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b53b9fb5573323484af9a19cf3f5bfe80760abba/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/config/v1beta1/types.go#L940-L945

or are not primitive fields (they are pointers), so both explicit true and false would be serialized:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b53b9fb5573323484af9a19cf3f5bfe80760abba/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/config/v1beta1/types.go#L984-L988

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b53b9fb5573323484af9a19cf3f5bfe80760abba/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/config/v1beta1/types.go#L994-L1001
@brandond I believe k3s can workaround the issue by setting both `--config` and `--config-dir`. I.e. `--config=etc/kubelet.conf --config-dir=etc/kubelet.conf.d`

As discussed above, we don't generate a config file. We generate only a config drop-in, as that allows more flexibility with regards to merging config files and flags provided by users.

Unfortunately there are some fine details around the different defaults that are set by the Kubelet when using a config file, vs the config drop-in directory, that are easy to miss.

title: Pods on very few worker nodes do not have network connectivity after control plane and calico upgrade
body:

@khteh  The behavior you're seeing is actually expected for headless services. When you create a headless service (clusterIP: None), Kubernetes doesn't create a service IP or perform port translation - it simply creates DNS entries that point directly to the pod IPs.

In your case:

Your service defines port 80, but your pod is listening on port 8000
The DNS resolution works correctly (resolving to 10.1.207.210)
But since there's no service proxy doing port translation, you need to use the actual container port (8000)
With regular ClusterIP services, the kube-proxy would handle mapping from service port 80 to target port 8000, but headless services don't use kube-proxy - they're just DNS entries.

If you want to access the service without specifying the port, you have two options:

1. Make your pod listen on port 80 to match the service definition
2. Change your service port to 8000 to match what the pod is listening on
Thanks for clarification.

title: kubectl drain no longer works with node accounts in Kubernetes 1.32
body:
### What happened?

Since Kubernetes 1.32, the AuthorizeNodeWithSelectors feature gate defaults to true. This leads to Nodes only being able to query Pods that are associated with that node. kubectl drain does not handle this gracefully; when run with node credentials, it will evict or terminate all pods, but then exit on a permission error as those pods, once successfully terminated or evicted, no longer have a relationship with that node and are thus not accessible to it via API.

### What did you expect to happen?

kubectl drain finishes cleanly after all Pods have been evicted or terminated, as it does on 1.31 or with the AuthorizeNodeWithSelectors feature gate set to false.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run kubectl drain on a node running Kubernetes 1.32 with default feature gate settings, using the node's own account for authorization.

title: Severe file copy slowdown in pod using Local PV after node reboot (resolved by pod recreation)
body:
### What happened?

We are using Local PersistentVolume (local PV) to mount a local directory to a pod. After a node reboot, the pod is still running, but performing file copy operations inside the pod (e.g., using `cp`) becomes very slow.

Using `strace -f -tt -T -p <PID>` to trace the cp process shows that `sendfile()` system calls are taking 0.7+ seconds per 16MB chunk:
```
15:02:53.949729 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.715818>
15:02:54.665935 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.731067>
15:02:55.397318 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.737302>
...

```

However, if we delete the pod and let it be recreated, the file copy speed returns to normal. sendfile() calls then complete in ~0.015 seconds:
```
15:04:38.006504 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.015368>
15:04:38.022146 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.015512>
...
```



### What did you expect to happen?

After node reboot, the pod using local PV should continue to perform file copy operations at normal speed without requiring a pod delete and recreate.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.Create a pod that mounts a local directory using local PersistentVolume.
2.Perform a file copy operation inside the pod (e.g., cp largefile /tmp/), observe performance is good.
3.Reboot the node where the pod is scheduled.
4.After the node is back and the pod is still running, repeat the file copy operation.
5.Observe that file copy is very slow.
6.Delete the pod, let it be recreated (same node), and copy files again — performance is back to normal.

title: Is it necessary to keep the Duration at the Cap value
body:
### What happened?

I'm encountering a scenario where a check operation needs to be executed at intervals of `1s, 2s, 4s... (doubling each time) up to a cap of 1 minute`. After reaching the 1-minute cap, the check operation should persistently run every 1 minute. So I try to implement it with following code
```go
backoff: &Backoff{
		Duration: time.Second,
		Factor:   2,
		Steps: math.MaxInt32,
		Cap:   time.Minute,
	}
```
But the current `wait.BackOff` implementation fails to achieve this behavior because once the `Cap` is reached, it immediately sets the `Step` field value to zero, thereby terminating the looped check operation. Therefore, is it necessary to add an option to ensure the `Duration` remains at the `Cap` value after reaching it?

title: Kubelet can host "phantom" pod upon etcd restore.
body:
### What happened?

Hi, we found a situation similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115325, while caused by etcd being restored to a previous snapshot, which "erased" a created pod.

Kubelet complains resource problem and fails newly scheduled pods, as if the original pod is still there (well, it is).

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should have some warning and ideally reconnect to apiserver and remove the "phantom" pod as a orphaned pod.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See https://github.com/tdihp/myakshack/tree/main/repros/phantompod for a tested working repro, while to describe on how to reproduce this in simple words:

1. take a etcd backup
2. provision a pod until it is running in kubelet
3. take etcd down, and restore it to backup
4. restart etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler, notice kubelet isn't restarted.
5. The pod will be gone, while will be running if we do crictl on the node.

title: Test tooling: agnhost pause command may exit with 0 occasionally
body:
### What happened?

The agnhost command may occasionally exit with 0 which is not the intention: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/78e9ba9d9ac70ceeadd90e95af553add0e2ed36e/test/images/agnhost/pause/pause.go#L37-L56

### What did you expect to happen?

Only exit with failure, 1 (sigint), 2 sigterm, if the traps are registered.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Compile the agnost image with the following changes to make it more likely to happen:
```
func pause(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
        fmt.Println("Paused")
        sigCh := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
        done := make(chan int, 1)
        signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGINT)
        signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGTERM)
        fmt.Println("Signals registered")
        go func() {
                sig := <-sigCh
                switch sig {
                case syscall.SIGINT:
                        fmt.Println("received SIGINT")
                        done <- 1
                        time.Sleep(time.Minute)
                        os.Exit(1)
                case syscall.SIGTERM:
                        fmt.Println("received SIGTERM")
                        done <- 2
                        time.Sleep(time.Minute)
                        os.Exit(2)
                }
        }()
        result := <-done
        fmt.Printf("exiting %d\n", result)
}
```
Such an image is here: https://hub.docker.com/repository/docker/mszadkow256/moje/tags/2.53-sleep-pause/sha2[…]de7b47e396a90e6ed9eaf66b0e3a66d6378211327fd18cbfd9deb090db06a

2. Run it `docker run --rm mszadkow256/moje:2.53-sleep-pause pause`
3. In another console send SIGTERM: `docker exec 60a273597124 kill 1` 
Issue: The pause command exists with 0 (check with `echo $?`



### Anything else we need to know?

This caused flakes in Kueue tests which was assuming the exit code is always a failure: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/4733

I think the intention of the code is 

```golang
func pause(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
        fmt.Println("Paused")
        sigCh := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
        done := make(chan int, 1)
        signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGINT)
        signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGTERM)
        fmt.Println("Signals registered")
        go func() {
                sig := <-sigCh
                switch sig {
                case syscall.SIGINT:
                        done <- 1
                case syscall.SIGTERM:
                        done <- 2
                }
        }()
        result := <-done
        fmt.Printf("exiting %d\n", result)
        os.Exit(result)
}
```

title: [Windows] HNS endpoints creation fails after remote HNS endpoints with same IP address were created
body:
### What happened?

When deploying Windows containers on Windows Nodes, some Windows containers fails to have network configuration inside like this:
```
S C:\> ipconfig /all

Windows IP Configuration

   Host Name . . . . . . . . . . . . : windows-server-iis-ltsc2022-58467d4759-vgzjr
   Primary Dns Suffix  . . . . . . . : 
   Node Type . . . . . . . . . . . . : Hybrid
   IP Routing Enabled. . . . . . . . : No
   WINS Proxy Enabled. . . . . . . . : No
```

This issue happens for Windows containers that got assigned the same IP address that was previously assigned to pods on Linux but were deleted later.

When we create a Pod on Linux and a `LoadBalancer` service type that refers to Linux pod, `kube-proxy` on Windows create HNS endpoints of Remote type. If we delete these Linux pods, IP addresses assigned to these pods are released and Remote HNS endpoints are deleted from Windows nodes.

When I deploy Windows pod, and if this Windows pod gets assigned the same IP as Linux pod, HNS endpoint for these Windows containers fails to be created causing networking issues inside Windows container.

This issue is a likely regression due to #124092

### What did you expect to happen?

All Windows containers should successfully create HNS endpoint and networking should work inside Windows containers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy kubernetes cluster with limited available IPs for pods on both Linux and Windows node.
2. Deploy Linux pods that consume almost all IPs.
3. Deploy service type LoadBalancer that refer to Linux pods, This will trigger `kube-proxy` to create Remote HNS endpoint on Windows. This Remote HNS endpoint will have Linux pod IP.
4. Scale down the Linux pods to 1.
5. Deploy Windows pods so that same IP address from Linux pod can be reassigned to Windows Pods.
6. HNS endpoints for Windows pods with same address will not be created.
7. Internet connectivity inside these Windows pod will fail.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

nodes.title: Fix for HNS local endpoint was being deleted instead of the remote endpoint.
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
The queriedEndpoints map keeps track of HNS endpoint information for Windows nodes. If two endpoints (one remote and one local) share the same IP within the Windows nodes, the second entry will overwrite the first in the map since the IP address serves as the key. If, unfortunately, the second endpoint happens to be a local one, any attempt by the proxier code to retrieve the remote endpoint for deletion will instead fetch the local endpoint, leading to its unintended removal.

The update ensures that when two endpoints with the same IP exist on a Windows node, the remote endpoint always takes precedence. This map is exclusively used for endpoint deletion, and since kube-proxy is primarily concerned with remote endpoints, local endpoint information holds little significance in this context.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #130963

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
<!--
If no, just write "NONE" in the release-note block below.

-->

title: API server reflector may lose events if TransformFromStorage fails
body:
### What happened?

Hi 👋 ,

I'm investigating an issue where create or update operations on `Secrets` are _randomly_ not reflected in the controller runtime client cache. We have observed this behaviour multiple times, in at least 3 different operators, all relying on the controller-runtime client, and one of them being the External Secrets Operator. As a result the controllers indefinitely attempt to reconcile the missed `Secrets` from their stale cache, perpetually getting `409` errors until they are manually restarted. These Secrets seem to be lost by the `Watch` mechanism, while they are successfully created (as confirmed by audit logs), and eventually available in a `List` result.

After some investigations I realized that when this problem occur we also have transient errors related to Secret decryption, for example:

```
watcher.go:471] failed to prepare current and previous objects: failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing
reflector.go:467] storage/cacher.go:/secrets: retrying watch of *core.Secret internal error: Internal error occurred: failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing
```

I have tried to understand how events are processed in `storage/etcd3/watcher.go`, more specifically here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L427-L437

IIUC when an error occurs, an "error event" is sent back to the reflector through a channel:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L469-L474


But IIUC we keep processing other incoming events? This leads me to wonder if there is not a situation where:

1. etcd watcher temporary fails to decrypt a Secret with `resourceVersion=V`, the error is sent to the reflector:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L737-L743

2. Assuming that `case apierrors.IsInternalError(err) && retry.ShouldRetry()` is true the reflector is going to run the `watchHandler` again:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L466-L468

3. Meanwhile, let's suppose that the etcd watcher managed to decrypt another `Secret`, with a different name and with `resourceVersion=V+1`, the result is sent to the watcher which calls `setLastSyncResourceVersion` with `V+1` as a value here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L791

Which feels wrong since `Secret` with `resourceVersion` `V` has not been observed yet?

I would like to know if this sounds like a possible scenario that may explain what we are observing. If not please let me know if you have any ideas that might explain it. Thanks!

We have observed this issue on K8s 1.30 (v1.30.10-eks-bc803b4) with the following libraries:
* k8s.io/api v0.32.2
* k8s.io/apimachinery v0.32.2
* k8s.io/client-go v0.32.2
* sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime v0.20.2

### What did you expect to happen?

I think I would expect the Secrets which suffered what could be a temporary decryption failure to be eventually reflected in the cache.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unfortunately, this happens randomly in our case 😕 That being said if I run the API Server in a dev environment and _temporarily_ return an error in the `TransformFromStorage` function for a specific `Secret`, I can observe that this `Secret` is never going to be sent to a client while other `Secrets` created at the same time are correctly reflected in the controller-runtime client.

### Anything else we need to know?

This part of the code is (really) new to me but I'm happy to help, so please let me know if there is anything else I should investigate!

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Server Version: v1.30.10-eks-bc803b4
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
* EKS (eks.23 / K8s 1.30) 
</details>


### OS version

_No response_

nodes.body: If the API server temporarily fails to decrypt a Secret, it does not queue the event for later retry. Instead, the error is sent through the watch error mechanism, causing a reconnection attempt.
If another event (maybe a different Secret) is processed before the reconnect, the `resourceVersion` is bumped.
Since watches in Kubernetes typically resume from the last `resourceVersion`, the missed event is effectively skipped.
To fix this issue the API server could buffer failed decryption events and retry them instead of dropping them immediately.
Or the reflector could ensure that objects skipped due to decryption errors are explicitly re-fetched in the next watch cycle.
/sig api-machinery

IIUC the event is lost because the reflector does not consider the error as critical enough to return immediately from the watch function. This decision leads the reflector to favor availability over consistency, and is taken because by default any error (if not an `apierrors.APIStatus` error) is converted into an "Internal Error":

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa35eff1b636f587f418f9cc16a020353735d125/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L638-L640

Would it be an option for the `TransformFromStorage` function to be smarter, and return a more "opinionated" error to suggest that this error must not be ignored? Something along the lines of:

```golang
diff --git a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go
index a20b10fc3cb..097a5840a03 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go
@@ -31,6 +31,7 @@ import (
        "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
        "golang.org/x/crypto/cryptobyte"
 
+       "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"
        utilerrors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors"
        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/uuid"
        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation"
@@ -196,7 +197,7 @@ func (t *envelopeTransformer) TransformFromStorage(ctx context.Context, data []b
                if err != nil {
                        span.AddEvent("DEK decryption failed")
                        span.RecordError(err)
-                       return nil, false, fmt.Errorf("failed to decrypt DEK, error: %w", err)
+                       return nil, false, errors.NewServiceUnavailable("DEK decryption failed")
                }
                span.AddEvent("DEK decryption succeeded")
```

IIUC in that case it would force the reflector to return from the watch function, and more importantly would avoid `lastSyncResourceVersion` to be set to the wrong value (including on the client side).

/cc @siyuanfoundation @serathius 
Would you be able to take a look at this? Thanks!
/triage accepted

@barkbay this is a great finding, here's a reproduction of the issue on an HA cluster:
1. Issue a watch to apiserver1 on secrets.
2. Make the KMS plugin unhealthy for apiserver1 to prevent it from decrypting and caching any new DEK seeds (seeds that it hasn't seen prior to this point or any newly generated seed by a peer apiserver).
3. Restart apiserver2 to make it generate a new DEK seed.
4. Issue a watch against apiserver2 on secrets.
5. Create a new secret against apiserver2 (in the example below this is demo-secret2 which was written with a DEK seed that apiserver1 doesn't have cached) and delete an existing secret against apiserver2 (in the example below this is demo-secret1 which apiserver1 does have cached).


Watch events for a client against apiserver1
```
% kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/default/secrets?watch=true"
...
{"type":"ADDED","object":{"kind":"Secret","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{"name":"demo-secret1","namespace":"default","uid":"1652748e-a307-4cea-a3b2-aa7282c95667","resourceVersion":"7434736","creationTimestamp":"2025-03-20T19:31:56Z","managedFields":[{"manager":"kubectl-create","operation":"Update","apiVersion":"v1","time":"2025-03-20T19:31:56Z","fieldsType":"FieldsV1","fieldsV1":{"f:data":{".":{},"f:dbPassword":{},"f:dbUser":{}},"f:type":{}}}]},"data":{"dbPassword":"cDRzc3cwcmQ=","dbUser":"cG9zdGdyZXM="},"type":"Opaque"}}
{"type":"DELETED","object":{"kind":"Secret","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{"name":"demo-secret1","namespace":"default","uid":"1652748e-a307-4cea-a3b2-aa7282c95667","resourceVersion":"7435455","creationTimestamp":"2025-03-20T19:31:56Z","managedFields":[{"manager":"kubectl-create","operation":"Update","apiVersion":"v1","time":"2025-03-20T19:31:56Z","fieldsType":"FieldsV1","fieldsV1":{"f:data":{".":{},"f:dbPassword":{},"f:dbUser":{}},"f:type":{}}}]},"data":{"dbPassword":"cDRzc3cwcmQ=","dbUser":"cG9zdGdyZXM="},"type":"Opaque"}}
```


Watch events for a client against apiserver2
```
% kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/default/secrets?watch=true"
...
{"type":"ADDED","object":{"kind":"Secret","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{"name":"demo-secret1","namespace":"default","uid":"1652748e-a307-4cea-a3b2-aa7282c95667","resourceVersion":"7434736","creationTimestamp":"2025-03-20T19:31:56Z","managedFields":[{"manager":"kubectl-create","operation":"Update","apiVersion":"v1","time":"2025-03-20T19:31:56Z","fieldsType":"FieldsV1","fieldsV1":{"f:data":{".":{},"f:dbPassword":{},"f:dbUser":{}},"f:type":{}}}]},"data":{"dbPassword":"cDRzc3cwcmQ=","dbUser":"cG9zdGdyZXM="},"type":"Opaque"}}
{"type":"ADDED","object":{"kind":"Secret","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{"name":"demo-secret2","namespace":"default","uid":"29efa04f-2df0-4edb-9a07-124201c37604","resourceVersion":"7435425","creationTimestamp":"2025-03-20T19:35:58Z","managedFields":[{"manager":"kubectl-create","operation":"Update","apiVersion":"v1","time":"2025-03-20T19:35:58Z","fieldsType":"FieldsV1","fieldsV1":{"f:data":{".":{},"f:dbPassword":{},"f:dbUser":{}},"f:type":{}}}]},"data":{"dbPassword":"cDRzc3cwcmQ=","dbUser":"cG9zdGdyZXM="},"type":"Opaque"}}
{"type":"DELETED","object":{"kind":"Secret","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{"name":"demo-secret1","namespace":"default","uid":"1652748e-a307-4cea-a3b2-aa7282c95667","resourceVersion":"7435455","creationTimestamp":"2025-03-20T19:31:56Z","managedFields":[{"manager":"kubectl-create","operation":"Update","apiVersion":"v1","time":"2025-03-20T19:31:56Z","fieldsType":"FieldsV1","fieldsV1":{"f:data":{".":{},"f:dbPassword":{},"f:dbUser":{}},"f:type":{}}}]},"data":{"dbPassword":"cDRzc3cwcmQ=","dbUser":"cG9zdGdyZXM="},"type":"Opaque"}}
```
In this example, the client for apiserver1 misses the create event for demo-secret2. It will not pick up the missed event on a new watch request because it received a subsequent event for the delete secret1 event. It seems like the desired behavior is that all watchers on the given resource should be closed if it TransformFromStorage fails.

The probability of this occurring increases during apiserver process terminations in an HA setup. This can occur after launching new apiservers + terminating the old apiservers because the apiserver KMS grpc client shuts down before watches are closed (even if the KMS provider itself isn't shutdown):
```
E0320 20:46:51.747007      12 transformer.go:164] "failed to decrypt data" err="failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing"
E0320 20:46:51.747169      12 watcher.go:567] failed to prepare current and previous objects: failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing
I0320 20:46:51.747281      12 reflector.go:489] storage/cacher.go:/secrets: retrying watch of *core.Secret internal error: Internal error occurred: failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing
```
Without setting shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period, it looks like the grpc client will close after around 10-20s whereas watches are allows to stay open for 1 minute after the shutdown sequence. In addition to the underlying issue with missing watch events, a mitigation to this issue would be to ensure the apiserver KMS grpc client stays healthy until all watchers are closed.
cc @liggitt
cc @deads2k

Any change here needs to consider both permanent and transient failure cases.

If there's permanent failures of TransformFromStorage, this intersects with https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-auth/3926-handling-undecryptable-resources

cc @enj @aramase 

Recent dramatically increased reliance on watch cache to serve reads (https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/956-watch-bookmark, https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/4988-snapshottable-api-server-cache, https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/4568-resilient-watchcache-initialization, https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/3157-watch-list) makes the impact much higher if a permanent TransformFromStorage error puts a reflector in a state where it will never succeed.

cc @wojtek-t @serathius

I was looking into how the KMS grpc client is closed and it looks like setting shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period to a non-zero value can help mitigate the risk of this occurring during apiserver shutdowns, specifically the situation when the KMS provider becomes unavailable while watches are still open.

Case 1: without setting shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period
- The apiserver respects shutdown-delay-duration, waits for non-long-running requests to drain, and does not wait for long-running requests to drain. 
- After running some tests, it looks like watches will be closed 1 minute after the shutdown-delay-duration whereas the "grpc: the client connection is closing" KMS error occurs before this 1 minute has passed. This is due to watches not being drained here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/71eb04295ad273d6de3bc484f2280c5c3954a4b3/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver.go#L660

Case 2: with setting shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period
- The apiserver respects shutdown-delay-duration, waits for non-long-running requests to drain, and waits for long-running requests to drain. 
- Once all requests have drained, it the shutdown handler will signal the InFlightRequestsDrained as completed: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/71eb04295ad273d6de3bc484f2280c5c3954a4b3/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver.go#L689
- My understanding is that this will signal the KMS grpc client to be closed here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4288af4dc80e71b7d91c5ec6ad4b1698839d52eb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/grpc_service.go#L88
- The context above is set plumbed through from the DrainedNotify which looks at the InFlightRequestsDrained signal: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4288af4dc80e71b7d91c5ec6ad4b1698839d52eb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/etcd.go#L297

Let me know if I have a misunderstanding but it looks like even setting 1s for this flag (or updating the shutdown logic to just close all watchers at that point without rate limiting which happens after 1 minute anyways) would reduce the chances of this happening against a shutting down apiserver.
I have opened #130991 to discuss potential changes to `--shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period`.

Thanks for the repro @natherz97.

This issue has the potential for data loss in API server watch cache and clients downstream. Given this could happen even outside of the shutdown case, we need a robust way to address the risk in the watcher itself (same way we do not allow continuing on a [compaction error](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd43c3d29d5203378ce456de9466597234a83e66/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/errors.go#L34) today).

Besides the issue @liggitt pointed above on differentiating transient (e.g KMS unavailable) and non-transient (e.g bit flip) decode errors, there's another serious issue here iiuc - watch events received from etcd may not be delivered to watch-cache in serial order when there's an error in event processing. While [processEvents](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa35eff1b636f587f418f9cc16a020353735d125/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L234) is calling [transform](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa35eff1b636f587f418f9cc16a020353735d125/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L441) on events serially, any error while transforming is handled by [sendError](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa35eff1b636f587f418f9cc16a020353735d125/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L568) that writes to a buffered errChan that is later read/processed async by [different goroutine](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa35eff1b636f587f418f9cc16a020353735d125/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L236-L259). While we close the resultChan eventually after translating the error to a an event and writing to that channel, subsequent events may have already been written. I think we should stop any further writes to resultChan once sendError is called (except for the error event itself).

Thanks for opening this bug. Just few thoughts from me:

> It seems like the desired behavior is that all watchers on the given resource should be closed if it TransformFromStorage fails.

I would split two things:
(a) the watch that is propagating the watchcache
(b) the watches opened against kube-apiserver

The primary question is why watch from (a) is not closed  - that's the part I don't fully understand.
Looking at the code - it actually should fail - modulo the bug @shyamjvs pointed above (that sendError is asynchronous). That seems like a very serious bug to fix.

But I still don't understand what really happens in the repro described above.
Let's for a moment assume that watch events are coming rarely and we're not exposed to races due to the above issue.

In this case, when we can't decrypt the event, the error is returned and that closes the watch propagating watchcache (an error event is send and the watch is closed - because each error is effectively closing the watch:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa35eff1b636f587f418f9cc16a020353735d125/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L236-L251 ).
And then resuming the watch should happen from the point of last event, so we will try to watch the event that previously closed decryption again.
What am I missing?

FWIW - I opened a WIP attempt for how the fix for the problem mentioned above can be addressed: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131020
  (FWIW - this is not watchcache specific and this exists even without watchcache)

But I'm fairly sure this is not the issue that repro shows - and that one I still don't understand what's happening.

Good point. The repro shared in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/130898#issuecomment-2741579482 actually stopped at:

```
E0320 20:46:51.747169      12 watcher.go:567] failed to prepare current and previous objects: failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing
I0320 20:46:51.747281      12 reflector.go:489] storage/cacher.go:/secrets: retrying watch of *core.Secret internal error: Internal error occurred: failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing
```

so we know the error [was sent](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa35eff1b636f587f418f9cc16a020353735d125/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L567-L568) to watch-A and cacher tried to restart it too? But that failed due to connection to KMS plugin closing due to the nature of the repro. @natherz97 maybe there are some more logs (say at higher verbosity) indicating RV at which cacher tried restarting the watch? Just to prove atleast the restart part is working fine.

@wojtek-t @shyamjvs I think I figured out the sequence of events in watcher.go that allows the reflector to miss a watch event by adding some additional logging. From the repro, we have a create event for secret2 followed by delete event for secret1.

serialProcessEvents thread:  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.32.3/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L436
- receives create for secret2 from incomingEventChan
- transform returned an error, it calls sendError which sends through errChan
- receives delete for secret1 from incomingEventChan
- successfully sends secret1 through resultChan, this will increment the RV for the reflector
- routine picks up <-wc.ctx.Done() in outer case and hits return statement (triggered from wc.cancel())

run thread: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.32.3/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L237
- reads from errChan and converts err to watch event from the transform error for secret2 
- successfully sends event through resultChan
- calls wc.cancel() + resultChanWG.Wait() (which triggers serialProcessEvents to stop)
- calls close(wc.resultChan)

Thread interleaving:
- serialProcessEvents: received create for secret2 from incomingEventChan
- serialProcessEvents: transform returned an error, it calls sendError which sends through errChan
- serialProcessEvents: received delete for secret1 from incomingEventChan
- serialProcessEvents: successfully sends secret1 through resultChan, this will increment the RV for the reflector
- run: reads from errChan and converts err to watch event from the transform error for secret2 
- run: successfully sends event through resultChan
- run: calls wc.cancel() + resultChanWG.Wait()
- serialProcessEvents: routine picks up <-wc.ctx.Done() in outer case and hits return statement
- run: calls close(wc.resultChan)

This thread interleaving confirms what Shyam called out above in this comment: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/130898#issuecomment-2744843973.

I think there's 2 cases:
1. If the create + delete happen in short succession before the watch is closed, we'll see the sequence of events above where we fail to observe the create event for secret2 but still increment reflector RV on delete for secret1.
2. If the create + delete occur over a longer period, eventually we will see the same sequence of events above but it may be on a later watch. If no other watch events occur after secret2 is created, the reflector will attempt to watch from the RV of the failed secret2 and continually fail and close the watch without bumping the RV as expected. As soon as the delete event occurs for secret1, it will trigger the same situation as above where incomingEventChan has 2 events. At this point, we will send the delete event for secret1 on resultChan before the create for secret2 which will increment the RV in the reflector and cause the missed event. As a result, we would recover without the missing event if no additional watch events occur before the KMS provider recovers.
Closing with https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131020 and the cherrypicks already merged.

title: Resources overwritten when using identical Group/Version in client-gen
body:
### What happened?

In [staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/client-gen/args/args.go#L129-L138](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0-alpha.3/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/client-gen/args/args.go#L129-L138), the `GroupVersionPackages()` function uses GroupVersion as map keys to store package paths. When multiple different API resources use the same Group and Version, the later-defined resources will overwrite earlier ones in the returned map.

### What did you expect to happen?

Resources with different package names but the same group names and versions should not be overwritten by each other.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Define two different API resources (e.g., `example` and `example2`)
2. Configure both resources with an identical group (e.g., `code-generator.k8s.io`) and version (e.g., `v1`)
3. Run `kube::codegen::gen_client` code generation

### Anything else we need to know?

During client code generation, only the last resource with a specific Group/Version combination is retained in the map returned by GroupVersionPackages(). This causes previously defined resources to be ignored or overwritten, resulting in incomplete client code generation.

The issue occurs in this implementation:
``` golang
func (args *Args) GroupVersionPackages() map[types.GroupVersion]string {
    res := map[types.GroupVersion]string{}
    for _, pkg := range args.Groups {
        for _, v := range pkg.Versions {
            // When two different resources have the same Group and Version, 
            // they will use identical keys in the map
            res[types.GroupVersion{Group: pkg.Group, Version: v.Version}] = v.Package
        }
    }
    return res
}
```
When multiple resources use the same Group and Version combination, later resources overwrite earlier ones in the map, causing data loss.

title: Job controller's race condition - Pod finalizer removal and job uncounted status update should work in separate reconcile
body:
### What happened?

Job controller accidentally created two pods even if the Job spec specifies in a busy cluster:

```
  parallelism: 1
  completions: 1
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 86400
  backoffLimit: 0
```

This is happening because when job controller is calculating the succeed pods, it's taking three inputs ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L892)):

1. The completion count from `Job.status.succeeded`
2. The existing succeed pods (if the finalizer is still present)
3. The uncounted completion count from `Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods`

Due to the current implementation where the job controller is refreshing both (2) and (3) in the same reconcile/sync process:

> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1165-L1167

The job controller may miscount the succeeded pods when the watch event for (3) hasn't reach the controller. A delayed watch event is fairly likely to happened in a busy cluster.

### What did you expect to happen?

The better implementation should be handling the refreshing of (2) and (3) in separate reconcile process:

(1) in the 1st reconcile, job controller should only refresh `Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods` while preserving the finalizers on the pods
(2) in the 2nd reconcile which is triggered by (1), job controller is safe to remove the finalizers from pods

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Any trivial job with 1 completion on a busy cluster should be able to reproduce the issue

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

All k8s versions I assume

### Cloud provider

Any

### OS version

Any

The following is a unit-test to emulate and reproduce when the pod leakage happens:

```go
func TestJobControllerRaceCondition(t *testing.T) {
	t.Cleanup(setDurationDuringTest(&syncJobBatchPeriod, fastSyncJobBatchPeriod))
	logger, ctx := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
	job1 := newJob(1, 1, 6, batch.NonIndexedCompletion)
	job1.Name = "job1"
	clientSet := fake.NewSimpleClientset(job1)
	//clientset := clientset.NewForConfigOrDie(&restclient.Config{Host: "", ContentConfig: restclient.ContentConfig{GroupVersion: &schema.GroupVersion{Group: "", Version: "v1"}}})
	fakeClock := clocktesting.NewFakeClock(time.Now())
	jm, informer := newControllerFromClientWithClock(ctx, t, clientSet, controller.NoResyncPeriodFunc, fakeClock)
	jm.podControl = &controller.RealPodControl{
		KubeClient: clientSet,
		Recorder:   testutil.NewFakeRecorder(),
	}
	jm.podStoreSynced = alwaysReady
	jm.jobStoreSynced = alwaysReady
 
	informer.Batch().V1().Jobs().Informer().GetIndexer().Add(job1)
	// 1st reconcile should create a new pod
	err := jm.syncJob(ctx, testutil.GetKey(job1, t))
	time.Sleep(time.Second)
 
	podIndexer := informer.Core().V1().Pods().Informer().GetIndexer()
	assert.NotNil(t, podIndexer)
	podList, err := clientSet.Tracker().List(
		schema.GroupVersionResource{Version: "v1", Resource: "pods"},
		schema.GroupVersionKind{Version: "v1", Kind: "Pod"},
		"default")
	assert.NotNil(t, podList)
	// manually adding the just-created pod from fake clientset memory to informer cache because informer is not started.
        // meanwhile, intentionally not adding the job status update to the informer cache to simulate the situation when the job watch event delayed.
	justCreatedPod := podList.(*v1.PodList).Items[0]
	justCreatedPod.Finalizers = nil
	justCreatedPod.Status.Phase = v1.PodSucceeded
	podIndexer.Add(&justCreatedPod)
	jm.addPod(logger, &justCreatedPod)
	
	// removing the just created pod from fake clientset memory, but the pod will remain inside informer cache
	clientSet.Tracker().Delete(		
		schema.GroupVersionResource{Version: "v1", Resource: "pods"},
		"default", "")
	// 2nd reconcile
	err = jm.syncJob(ctx, testutil.GetKey(job1, t))
	time.Sleep(time.Second)
	podList, err = clientSet.Tracker().List(
		schema.GroupVersionResource{Version: "v1", Resource: "pods"},
		schema.GroupVersionKind{Version: "v1", Kind: "Pod"},
		"default")
 
	// no pod should be created, but it will fail here
	assert.True(t, podList.(*v1.PodList).Items == 0)
}
```

title: kube-proxy: net.InterfaceAddrs may return error due to a race condition, causing the Nodeport Service to be inaccessible
body:
### What happened? In our production environment, which verson is 1.24.4 1. kube-proxy's error log: 2024-12-09T07:35:24.325300135+08:00 E1209 07:35:24.325193 1 proxier.go:1131] "Failed to get node IP address matching nodeport cidr" err="error listing all interfaceAddrs from host, error: route ip+net: no such network interface" 2. Then the nodeport service's backend pod on this node cannot be accessible by the Nodeport Service. 3. On the save time, in this node's /var/log/message, the log is: Dec 9 07:35:24 VM-96-121-tencentos containerd: 2024-12-09T07:35:24+08:00 [info] cmdDel: {containerId c915c615cb43c0f7711d125e39e722581384bc45b3453e3c3c79ebe5ed994e71, netNs /var/run/netns/cni-278204fe-6400-6354-982f-ae2299bfae17, ifName eth0, args K8S_POD_INFRA_CONTAINER_ID=c915c615cb43c0f7711d125e39e722581384bc45b3453e3c3c79ebe5ed994e71;K8S_POD_UID=0a3c7874-54ae-4ec6-b4a5-b5c3b9d63a12;IgnoreUnknown=1;K8S_POD_NAMESPACE=bkmonitor-operator;K8S_POD_NAME=bcs-blackbox-job-073518-f8n4c, path /opt/cni/bin, stdinData {"capabilities":{"bandwidth":true,"portMappings":true},"cniVersion":"0.3.1","defaultDelegates":"tke-bridge","kubeconfig":"/etc/kubernetes/tke-cni-kubeconfig","logLevel":"info","name":"multus-cni","type":"multus"}}, , ### What did you expect to happen? The Nodeport Service should be accessible. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? In the latest version, it also have the same problem. 1, syncProxyRules->GetNodeIPs->net.InterfaceAddrs()->interfaceAddrTable(which is in interface_linux.go for Linux)->syscall.NetlinkRIB(syscall.RTM_GETADDR, syscall.AF_UNSPEC) is called. 2. Then an interface is delete by CNI. 3. Then interfaceAddrTable(which is in interface_linux.go) call interfaceTable(which is in interface_linux.go)->syscall.NetlinkRIB(syscall.RTM_GETLINK, syscall.AF_UNSPEC) The key point is that, RTM_GETADDR's return have the delete interface, but the RTM_GETLINK's return donot have the deleted interface. 4. Then in interfaceAddrTable->addrTable will return err. 5. Then the syncProxyRules will not write correct forward configuration because the GetNodeIPs's return donot have any ip. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version # paste output here ``` This production environment cluster version is v1.24.4 But any version have the same problem.

title: Kube scheduler has a confusing error message when scheduling pods that use claims with `ReadWriteOncePod` access mode
body:
### What happened?

When we deploy a claim like:
```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: ebs-claim
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOncePod
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 4Gi
```

And then deploy two pods:
```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: centos
    command: ["/bin/sh"]
    args: ["-c", "while true; do echo $(date -u) >> /data/out.txt; sleep 5; done"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: persistent-storage
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: persistent-storage
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: ebs-claim
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app2
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: centos
    command: ["/bin/sh"]
    args: ["-c", "while true; do echo $(date -u) >> /data/out.txt; sleep 5; done"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: persistent-storage
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: persistent-storage
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: ebs-claim
```
Second pod is rightfully not scheduled.
It has the following error message:
```
 k describe po app2

Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  5s    default-scheduler  0/5 nodes are available: 5 node has pod using PersistentVolumeClaim with the same name and ReadWriteOncePod access mode. preemption: 0/5 nodes are available: 5 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.
  Warning  FailedScheduling  2s    default-scheduler  0/5 nodes are available: 5 node has pod using PersistentVolumeClaim with the same name and ReadWriteOncePod access mode. preemption: 0/5 nodes are available: 5 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.
```
This error message is misleading - there are no 5 nodes that have pods using this PersistentVolumeClaim.

Error message comes from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.30.5/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumerestrictions/volume_restrictions.go#L55.
It's set in the following method - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.30.5/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumerestrictions/volume_restrictions.go#L280
It's raised upon calling the `Filter` method - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.30.5/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumerestrictions/volume_restrictions.go#L314

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect that we get an error message that reads something like:
```
  Warning  FailedScheduling  5s    default-scheduler  0/5 nodes are available: 5 nodes were not able to schedule a pod using PersistentVolumeClaim <PVC-Name> name, ReadWriteOncePod access mode. preemption: 0/5 nodes are available: 5 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.
```

or similar message, that points the operator to the actual reason for not scheduling the pod.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Build a cluster with 3 or more nodes and apply the following manifests:
```ymal
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: ebs-claim
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOncePod
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 4Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: centos
    command: ["/bin/sh"]
    args: ["-c", "while true; do echo $(date -u) >> /data/out.txt; sleep 5; done"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: persistent-storage
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: persistent-storage
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: ebs-claim
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app2
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: centos
    command: ["/bin/sh"]
    args: ["-c", "while true; do echo $(date -u) >> /data/out.txt; sleep 5; done"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: persistent-storage
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: persistent-storage
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: ebs-claim
```

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Namespace deletion does not trigger container lifecycle hooks
body:
### What happened?

I want to ensure that certain commands are run on graceful deletion of a pod, so I have set up a container lifecycle prestop hook to do so. Deleting the pod does trigger the prestop hook as expected; however, when deleting the namespace that the pod is in, I would expect this to also be a graceful shutdown event, which should trigger the prestop hook, but this does not happen. In addition, helm uninstalling our helm chart with the relevant statefulset has the same issue. See the test example below where we have setup RBAC for kubectl access within the container:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: <>
  namespace: <>
  labels:
    component: <>
    app: <>
spec:
  ...
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: testContainer
          image: <>
          lifecycle:
           preStop:
             exec:
               command:
                  - /bin/bash
                  - -c
                  - "kubectl label cm test-configmap -n test-prestop-hook testlabel=8 --overwrite"
             
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Prestop hook should be triggered by namespace deletion. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Bring up a pod with a container that has a prestop hook configured
2. Exec into the pod and label the ConfigMap to see that it works (no RBAC or image issues)
3. Delete the namespace that the pod is in (expected to trigger the prestop hook)
4. Wait 30 seconds and see that the prestop hook did not run, configmap label did not change to `testlabel: "8"`

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.28.1
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Server Version: v1.29.10-eks-7f9249a
```

</details>

> when deleting the namespace that the pod is in, I would expect this to also be a graceful shutdown event which should trigger the prestop hook,

When a namespace is deleted, K8s uses a namespace finalizer to clean up all resources. also K8s might clean up resources like Pods, bypassing some of the usual deletion procedures, including triggering the preStop hook.

>  but this does not happen. In addition, helm uninstalling our helm chart with the relevant statefulset has the same issue.

Similarly, when Helm uninstalls are used, resources like `Statefulsets` and `Pods` are deleted as part of the Helm release cleanup.

Try to add a _**finalizer**_ to the `Pods` or `StatefulSet` to delay their deletion. check your `StatefulSet` or `Pod` has a sufficiently large `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to allow the prestop hook to execute.
Namespace deletion does not bypass pod finalizers, it issues normal pod deletions, then waits for the pods to terminate and be deleted by the kubelet normally

> also K8s might clean up resources like Pods, bypassing some of the usual deletion procedures, including triggering the preStop hook.

That is not accurate, namespace deletion triggers normal deletion of pods.

What is more likely is that namespace deletion also deletes all objects in the namespace, including the service account and rbac role bindings, which can result in service account credentials for the pod being invalidated or forbidden if they attempt to be used to make API requests

Hi, I've tried to reproduce it.
The preStop hook seems to have been triggered correctly.

1. Create test namespace.

```bash
$ kubectl create ns test
```

2. Prepare the pod manifest including preStop.

`test-pod.yaml`
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-pod
  namespace: test
  labels:
    app: test-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ubuntu
    image: ubuntu:22.04
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while :; do sleep 10; done"]
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo 'Pod is terminating' > /host-tmp/output"]
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /host-tmp
      name: host-tmp
  volumes:
  - name: host-tmp
    hostPath:
      path: /tmp
```

3. Create the test-pod.

```bash
$ kubectl apply -f test-pod.yaml 

$ kubectl get pod -n test
NAME       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
test-pod   1/1     Running   0          14s
```

4. Delete test namespace.
```bash
$ kubectl delete ns test
namespace "test" deleted
```

5. Check `/tmp` of Node where pod's preStop command will output a file.

```bash
# cat /tmp/output
Pod is terminating
```

> What is more likely is that namespace deletion also deletes all objects in the namespace, including the service account and rbac role bindings, which can result in service account credentials for the pod being invalidated or forbidden if they attempt to be used to make API requests

Is there any way to ensure that these resources are removed after the preStop hook call? That would explain why our tests have not worked while @mochizuki875 's did. Regardless, not having RBAC (or even network policies) would seem to greatly limit the capability of the prestop hook (and would not be very useful for our case).

title: CVE-2024-7598: Network restriction bypass via race condition during namespace termination
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) - **Low** (3.1)

A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where a malicious or compromised pod could bypass network restrictions enforced by network policies during namespace deletion. The order in which objects are deleted during namespace termination is not defined, and it is possible for network policies to be deleted before the pods that they protect.  This can lead to a brief period in which the pods are running and accepting network connections, but the network policies restrictions are not applied.

### Am I vulnerable?

All clusters that rely on network policies may be vulnerable.  Run the following command to see if network policies are in use:

```
kubectl get networkpolicies.networking.k8s.io --all-namespaces
```

#### Affected Versions

kube-apiserver >= v1.3

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

This issue can be mitigated by:

- Manually deleting pods and workload resources that orchestrate pods before starting namespace deletion

- Adding finalizers to network policies to prevent them from being deleted until the pods that they protect have been deleted first. The following proof-of-concept controller automates this process:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/network-policy-finalizer 

#### Fixed Versions

- None. A longer term comprehensive fix is proposed in the following KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5095 

### Detection

Users of network policies may be able to detect abuse via network logs.  The exact details of this process are environment specific.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by John McGuinness @s1xtw03 and Aaron Coffey @aaroncoffey.

The issue was coordinated by:
